Shell Hell

By: Sophia Phirippides | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The Wild Coast, pristine untouched, until now. Seismic surveys conducted by Shell threaten to destabilise the delicate balance of an oceanic ecosystem, unique to South African shores.

Unique Selling Point:
Royal Dutch Shell is adamant to perform 3D Seismic Surveys on the Wild Coast beginning on the 1st of December 2021. This is despite a huge outcry and intensive negotiations with lawyers on behalf of concerned organisations. On the 26th of November Shell refused to bend, and now an urgent interdict to stop the exploration is underway.

The Green Connection is particularly concerned about the timing of this seismic survey phase, which is understood to still fall within the migration season for hump-backed whales and warned it could also endanger juvenile turtles coming down the coast in the Agulhas current and into the survey area over the five-month period.

Shell’s own 2013 Environmental Management Programme (EMPr) states that it should try to “avoid surveying during December when humpback whales may still be moving through the area on their return migrations”, McDaid pointed out.

Scientists are at loggerheads, some like Kevin Cole say, that not enough research has been conducted to really understand the impact of seismic surveys, and Simon Elwen who was involved in the original EMPr says that it’s not as devastating as people are making out, although there are behavioural impacts on marine life but according to him, they are short term. He does admit that Zooplankton are dramatically depleted, but rejuvenate easily, and that no studies have been done on the impact of coral. He says these surveys are done the world over and we have seen no real decimation of the oceans. There are many scientists that disagree.

We investigate the science and the motivation behind Shell’s move on our shores.

Summary:
After a 9 year hiatus, exploration for gas reserves through 3D seismic surveys is planned to start on the 1st of December this year, by Royal Dutch Shell PLC, on South Africa’s Wild Coast.
The scope of the survey will cover more than 6000 square kms at depths of 700m to 3000m. The exploration area is about 20 kilometers from the coastline at it’s closest point. Shell plans to embark on this seismic survey off the coast between Morgan Bay in the south and Port St Johns in the North. Over 150 000 South Africans have put pen to paper and signed a petition against this invasion of our shores. More protests are planned and marine biologists and activists are ready to serve an urgent interdict to try and stop this. But Shell says it’s within it’s legal right to conduct this survey based on an EMPr conducted in 2013.

This is especially pertinent in light of the fact that at the COP26 conference an $8,5 Billion deal was signed to help South Africa move away from reliance on fossil fuels, and Royal Dutch Shell has been ordered to reduce its emission by 45% by 2030 compared to 2019 levels. The case was brought against Shell by Friends of the Earth Netherlands, a climate advocacy group that has waged similar lawsuits in the past to accelerate global climate action. Shell plans to appeal the decision. The ruling requires the company to transform its business model worldwide, cutting emissions both for its own operations and the products it sells.

Basically the company is being forced to reduce its production and sale of fossil fuels, so why is Shell continuing its exploration on South African shores? Surveys of this nature can take up to 20 years to become drilling sites should gas be discovered and this is at a time that the world is moving away from fossil fuel energy. So who stands to benefit and who stands to lose? We investigate the long term effects of this decision.

Further information:
Nearly 200 concerned environmental defenders arrived at the Cape Town Waterfront on November 21 to protest against Shell’s seismic testing vessel Amazon Warrior, as it made its way into Cape Town harbour. The Amazon Warrior was commissioned by Shell to conduct seismic testing off the Wild Coast, in the Eastern Cape, stretching from the Kei river to the uMtamvuna river on the border of KwaZulu-Natal.

The vessel will conduct seismic surveys for an estimated five months.

This is an incredibly sensitive narrow coastal shelf along the East Coast of South Africa which is home to some of the most undisturbed natural areas and Marine reserves in the country including Dwesa, Cwebe and Hluleka reserves.

Not only this but the Wild Coast is notorious for some of the most extreme weather conditions and is recognised as one of the most treacherous coasts in the world due to its narrow continental shelf, strong ocean currents and severe wind conditions which have caused many ships to be lost over the years. Any future installation of oil rigs would place the entire coastline at risk of environmental destruction if anything were to happen in these treacherous waters.

Shell Exploration and Production SA which is a part of Royal Dutch Shell Plc issued a statement earlier this year, on their “Drive for net-zero emissions…” which outlines their stated objective of reducing their carbon footprint whilst supporting low environmental impact products, this surely doesn’t form part of that objective.

Shell has issued a statement:

Shell Downstream South Africa (Pty) Corporate Reputation and Media Relations spokesperson Pam Ntaka, said a full stakeholder consultation process was undertaken as part of the development of the EMPr for this project in 2013.

“Furthermore, the Environmental Authorisation was obtained for this project in 2014,” Ntaka said.

“… An Environmental Compliance audit was undertaken in 2020 by independent specialists to confirm that the controls and mitigation measures outlined in the EMPr were still sufficient and valid.”

“… The audit report confirmed that these requirements were still sufficient and valid for this project to be taken forward. We can confirm we are operating within our legal right and we believe we have met all our obligations concerning the survey,” Ntaka said.

“… Shell had a long experience in collecting seismic data and the welfare of wildlife was a major factor in the stringent controls it uses, strictly following the international guidelines of the Joint Nature Conservation Committee. We take great care to prevent or minimize impacts on fish, marine mammals and other wildlife. This is an exercise to collect data to help us understand if there is oil/gas or not. This is not a drilling exercise.”

The Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment (DFFE) on November 22 said Mineral Resources and Energy Minister Gwede Mantashe was responsible for the administration of the Mineral and Petroleum Resources Development Act (MPRDA) and that Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment Minister Barbara Creecy was, therefore, not mandated to consider an application or to make a decision on the authorisation of a seismic survey being undertaken by oil and gas multinational Shell.

“The impact of the seismic survey to be undertaken by Shell and [impact investment organisation] Impact Africa has been authorised under the MRPDA, which, under Section 39 (2) of the MPRDA requires the submission of an environmental management plan, which is to assess and evaluate the environmental impacts of the activity.”

“… Since the coming into effect of the One Environment System on December 8, 2014, the application process for the seismic surveys was finalised. All decisions made under the MPRDA at the time remain valid and binding until set aside by a court of law,” the DFFE said in a statement.

ENVIRONMENTAL MANAGEMENT PLAN
Meanwhile, these marine protection practices during seismic surveying align with the findings and recommendations of an unrelated ‘Environmental Management Plan for a reconnaissance permit to undertake a speculative two-dimensional (2D) seismic survey in the Durban Basin off the East Coast of South Africa’, prepared by local environmental consultancy CCA Environmental for State-owned petroleum exploration Petroleum Agency South Africa (Pasa) in October 2013.

This 2013 environmental management plan (EMP) said that, in summary, the majority of the impacts associated with the seismic survey would be of short-term duration and limited to the immediate survey area. As a result, the majority of the impacts associated with the seismic survey are considered to be of very low to low significance after mitigation.

“The two key issues identified in this study relate to the potential impact on turtles and marine mammals, including physiological injury and behavioural avoidance, as a result of seismic noise; and the potential impact on the fishing industry, including vessel interaction, disruption to fishing operations and reduced catch, owing to the presence of the survey vessel, potential fish avoidance of the survey area and changes in feeding behaviour,” the report's authors said.

“Although most of the impacts on turtles and cetaceans [whales, dolphins and porpoises] are assessed to have very low to low significance with mitigation, the impact could be of much higher significance owing to the limited understanding of how short-term effects of seismic surveys relate to longer term impacts,” the report highlighted.

“For example, if a sound source displaces a species from an important feeding or breeding area for a prolonged period, impacts at the population level could be more significant. In order to mitigate the potential impact on turtles and cetaceans it is recommended that the proposed seismic survey be planned to avoid key turtle nesting periods, from October to March, with peak nesting during December and January, and cetacean migration and breeding periods from the beginning of June to end of November.

“Thus, from an ecological perspective, the proposed survey should be undertaken from mid-March to the end of May. However, should the applicant require a longer survey period, that is early March to mid-June, the survey programme should be scheduled to avoid inshore areas during early March and the southern area during June”, the CCA Environmental 2013 EMP said.


TREATMENT AND APPROACH

I have spoken to both Kevin Cole, Natural Scientist and Simon Elwen, Marine Biologist who have differing opinions of how serious the impact is of seismic surveys. Although Simon Elwen is still advising the legal team who are bringing about the interdict against Shell, so clearly he is not that comfortable with it.

I have been approached by many organisations who are willing to assist in filming protests etc and have been offered a seat on the Bateleurs on the 5th of December where there will be protests along the coast. I can make a plan to have those filmed even if I don’t take that seat.

Interviews with both scientists as well as concerned citizens. There is also an international scientist I am trying to get hold of who has done a study on how seismic blasiting devastates the ocean’s zooplankton, which are critical food sources for marine mammals: Francine Kershaw, Staff Scientist. Marine Mammals, Oceans Division, Nature Program, USA.

Environmental protection and small-scale fishing lobby organisation The Green Connection strategic lead Liz McDaid said Shell has used a legal loophole, as no environmental impact assessment was required in 2013 and this authorisation was being used to justify its actions in 2021. Liz was involved in halting the nuclear deal, and she is concerned about the impact on fishing. She is willing to speak to us.


Judy Mann International Advisor for aquariums around the world, and a member of the South African Association for Marine Biological Research.

Sinegugu Zukulu – Activist Wild Coast – Amadiba Crisis Committee, an initiator of the protests for the 5th of December. He is an internationally recognised environmentalist and cultural expert.

Nonhle Mbuthuma – Activist against mining. (Has been involved in the struggle against mining in Xolobeni for years).

Ricky Stone – Attorney for bringing about the interdict on behalf of various organisations. I have been in contact with him and he is passing on information, although right now they are busy with the urgent interdict, but he is willing to be interviewed.

Another element I am exploring is following the money, what I know so far but still need to verify is that ANC owns 51% of Thebe and Thebe has 28% of Shell Downstream. I have to look deeper into that.

Press Release:


Globally the time for oil and gas exploration is running out and South Africa's oceans have been carved up - with seismic surveys mapping out our oceans - the Wild Coast is marked. Can its unique marine life remain unscathed?


Script:


Shots of underwater sea life (whale song) whales, dolphin sea creatures swimming…
Simon: Yeah, absolutely. The oceans are incredibly noisy.
// BEAT!!! ANIMALS
Simon: A lot of the animals that live on the water, communicate acoustically
// BEAT// ANIMALS
Simon: And that's because sound travels better than anything else underwater,
//BEAT//ANIMALS
Music visuals


INTERRUPT WITH LOUD ENGINE NOISE OF THE BOAT..CONTINUE NOISE OF BOAT.. UNDER LINK AND FADE OUT UNDER


LINK: Most of us are super sensitive to noise, be it to the neighbour playing loud music, the guy in the four-by-four hooting behind us. What do we know about noise underneath the water affecting marine life?


VO: The voices of marine experts can give us an inkling
Simon: What's a core focus with marine mammals is that they use sound also for navigation, because the dolphins and the beaked whales, they echolocate.
VO: Marine biologist Dr Simon Elwen, director of Seasearch, studies the behaviour and acoustic communication of these sound-sensitive beings.
Simon: They use sound to find food as well as to communicate with other individuals.


SEISMIC BANG!!!
VO:-Now what happens if this connection gets disrupted?


AIRGUNS BLASTING IN THE WATER


VO: Disrupted by 3D Seismic survey airguns fired from a ship into the water - Exploring the ocean bed for oil and gas.
//BEAT//BLASTS
Moving along a straight line gathering data, each seismic array pulse emits a sound that lasts less than 0.1 seconds at source and is repeated every 10 to 20 seconds.


// BEAT// WITH BLAST
Simon: And these, make an incredibly loud noise in the region of 200 decibels underwater,

VO: On land 200 decibels is louder than a jet engine taking off, but in water, the amplification, reception, and experience of sound are varied across species, because each is sensitive to different frequencies.


Derek: We going to look at some seals. I mean, how would they be affected by those air guns?
Simon: So if animals do have their hearing injured, that is obviously quite a negative impact. They use it in their day-to-day communication for mothers to find pups and vice versa


Derek: Simon, I'm trying to equate this to living in a block of apartments with a neighbor's drilling on his wall every 10 seconds. I’d go crazy!
Simon: And it really gets complicated when you're looking at whole ecosystems, you know, the loud noise like drilling next door, it might not kill you, but it might make you use that room less or, or
Derek:.. move somewhere else,
Simon: or even just eat a little bit less every day. And that that can become really important for species that are on the edge or endangered.
//BEAT// SOUND UP PROTESTS.


LINK: When South Africans heard about the 3d seismic surveys along the pristine wild coast, there was an outcry against the possible impact on marine life and that reverberated across the country.


VO: Petroleum giant Shell SA was embarking on a five-month exploration for oil and gas starting in December 2021, spanning 6000 square kilometres.


Neville: The next thing I saw, there was 1000s of people on that beach, you know, and the people were singing and dancing and chanting.
SOUND UP DEMONSTRATIONS


VO: Community coordinator for the Green Connection, Neville van Rooy was on the ground.


Neville: And it was communities from the area that came out. because our livelihood is connected to the ocean, our culture is connected to the ocean, our heritage is connected to the ocean.


VO: Shell's failure to consult with some small-scale fishing communities and directly affected people in the area tipped the scales. On the 28th of December last year a court stopped the seismic survey in its tracks.
But this was not the end of the legal process, Shell is appealing. Attorney Wilmien Wicomb is representing the communities.


Derek: So we’re celebrating a battle, but the war isn't over?
Wilmien: That's certainly the case. Although I do think it was quite a punch in the nose for Shell.


VO: How this clash unfolds hinges on an Environmental Authorisation //BEAT//- which Shell does not have. This only became law in December 2014 under the National Environmental Management Act, NEMA.


Phindile: So that Shell authorization, was applied for and granted under the MPRDA, as was the legislation at that time


VO: Regulating the industry is the Petroleum Agency South Africa, PASA. CEO Phindile Masangane maintains the 2013 permit is valid


Phindile: So we could not have granted them authorization under an existing legislation, and then turn around and say, Actually, you've got to redo it, because now we've got new regulations. The Department of the Environment also agrees with us in this instance.


VO: But one doesn't have to look far to see there is more to the relationship between Shell and the governing party. Even though this permit is for Shell's upstream business which involves exploration and production, it could be argued when it comes to shareholding there may be a conflict of interest.
The Batho Bhatho Trust, an investment vehicle for the ANC, is about a 46 percent shareholder of Thebe Investment Corp, and Thebe owns 28% of Shell's downstream business, the processing aspect of oil and gas, in South Africa.
In December, the Batho Batho Trust donated R15 million to bail out the ANC to pay its salaries.
We put it to Hloniphizwe Mtolo, Country Chair of Shell South Africa.


Derek: There is a financial connection between Shell and the ANC/government and they regulate your permit. Surely your international compliance officers must be concerned about a conflict of interest.
Hloniphizwe: We dispute very strongly the connection between Shell, the ANC, and government. What we do in terms of permitting, we follow the rules to the letter
Derek: It's a fine line, isn't it?
Hloniphizwe: Not in this particular case, In this particular case. We are looking at a shareholder who is working with a different part of the business and we are working on upstream.
Derek: But basically if Shell thrives, so does the ANC/Government, simple as that.
Hloniphizwe: We don't know that, and we don't believe that. But we believe that if this activity is successful South Africa will benefit


Wilmien: On the face of it, there's a serious conflict. But it has not arisen in any of the cases but, you know, watch this space.


Phindile: To try and find a link between any commercial relationship between the ANC and Thebe investment, as well as this production, right, I think I think it is stretching it.


LINK: Shell believes that they have complied with the conditions of the exploration permit and have taken enough precautions to mitigate any irreparable environmental damage.


Hloniphizwe: South Africa, in the last five years, there has been at least 12 seismic surveys that have been done. And all of those were done safely.


Hloniphizwe: The survey that we've started, we've done at least 14%, of what we wanted to do. And there has been absolutely no harm to the environment.


VO: The exclusion zone is meant to lessen damage to sea life. Shell has extended it beyond the compulsory 500 meters to 800 meters


Hloniphizwe That means that if an animal gets into this exclusion zone, the actual activity gets stopped. On a 24 hour basis, this zone is monitored. This survey that we were conducting in the wild coast is, has the lowest sound levels of any seismic survey that's been conducted in the past.


VO: But these mitigations are not enough for Dr Jean Harris who leads the marine programme Wild Oceans for Wild Trust.


Jean: We know from scientific studies where trained observers were looking for humpback whales that up to 40% were being missed. So what's happening to the rest of them?


VO: Wild Oceans was concerned when Shell decided to start the Seismic survey in December - at the tail end of the Humpback whale migration.


Jean: Reported evidence is that animals can lose connection with each other between, for example, a humpback whale and her calf. So it would have been much more responsible to start the survey in January, and then to move through to May at maximum.


VO: Elwen insists more research is needed for South African waters. He is also frustrated by public misconceptions on the impact of seismic surveys


Simon: They have not been linked clearly to killing whales and dolphins, they clearly have behavioural impacts they mask the communication of animals, there are many negative impacts, but it doesn't result in mass strandings of animals
VO: We dropped anchor in a quiet stretch of sea to listen on hydrophones to what's going on beneath.


Simon: You can still hear the ship in the background. And you can also hear crackling noise and that crackling's snapping shrimp
SOUND UP: DEREK LISTENING TO CRACKLING SHRIMP -
SEA SEARCH SOUND LIBRARY / Snapping Shrimp from remote location (Vema Seamount) - Sea Search Sound Library.mp3
Derek: I can hear the crackling.


VO: A reminder of the less audible and less visible creatures in the path of seismic surveys. Amongst them - zooplankton, an integral part of marine ecosystems. // In an Australian 2017 study published in Nature Ecology & Evolution, the devastating effects on zooplankton could be seen up to a 1.2-kilometre range.


Jean: the zooplankton, the small crustacea, and other species, which are the bottom of the food web. If you look at what they look like, after the shockwave has come through, there was, dead dead ones, damaged ones, indicating that, you'd have a mortality or death on those species.


VO: Wrong place, wrong time. Many marine animals could find themselves in the seismic danger zone, like critically endangered turtle species whose nestlings are swept along the Cape Agulhas current in the months of January to March.


Derek: There's also seen to be harmful effects on dolphins, turtles, and other sea creatures.
Hloniphizwe 31:28 From our evidence, there hasn't been any damage to those other creatures, we take great care in making sure that if there is any impact, it is impact that is as small as possible.
Derek: Mr. Mtolo, nobody's doing turtle tracking surveys, post your seismic operations. So we don't really know,
Hloniphizwe: What we do do, after the survey is completed, is to go back there and investigate if there's any any damage that has taken place. We do that with each and every one of the surveys that we do.
Derek: Do you really?
Hloniphizwe: We do
Derek: With a separate ship?
Hloniphizwe: Yeah, it would be a post-survey ship.
Derek: Can you give us examples of some of the ships that go in afterwards?
Hloniphizwe: We can, I can get you that information.


VO: But the devil's in the detail - on request for clarification after the interview it appears Mtolo was mistaken, there is no post-survey ship. Shell says all monitoring and reporting is in real-time from the vessels conducting the actual survey because they're always on the move.
So without any reliable data after the survey ship has left the area, the knock-on effects are hard to quantify.


LINK: You have to ask the question, why is the exploration for oil and gas which can take up to a decade or more, and encourages the use of fossil fuels being supported by government?


Phindile: It is Eskom the operator of the grid, that is saying it is very, very important for them to bring sufficient gas generated electricity to stabilise the grid.


VO: And government wants South Africa to have its own supply, under the Gas Master Plan, transitioning from an electricity supply system dominated by coal, to renewable energy supplemented by gas.
So even though South Africa committed to reducing its Carbon Footprint in global climate agreements, it has carved up its oceans for large-scale oil and gas exploration.


Wilmien: No one is taking a step back and trying to understand the cumulative impact of all these different permits. They're looking at them one by one. And that I think is really going to be a disaster.


VO: Well we've reached our destination - Seal Island -
A Priceless haven

Seismic surveys conducted by Shell threaten to destabilise the delicate balance of an oceanic ecosystem, unique to South African shores. Unique Selling Point: Royal Dutch Shell is adamant to perform 3D Seismic Surveys on the Wild Coast beginning on the 1st of December 2021. This is despite a huge outcry and intensive negotiations with lawyers on behalf of concerned organisations. On the 26th of November Shell refused to bend, and now an urgent interdict to stop the exploration is underway. The Green Connection is particularly concerned about the timing of this seismic survey phase, which is understood to still fall within the migration season for hump-backed whales and warned it could also endanger juvenile turtles coming down the coast in the Agulhas current and into the survey area over the five-month period. Shell’s own 2013 Environmental Management Programme (EMPr) states that it should try to “avoid surveying during December when humpback whales may still be moving through the area on their return migrations”, McDaid pointed out. Scientists are at loggerheads, some like Kevin Cole say, that not enough research has been conducted to really understand the impact of seismic surveys, and Simon Elwen who was involved in the original EMPr says that it’s not as devastating as people are making out, although there are behavioural impacts on marine life but according to him, they are short term. He does admit that Zooplankton are dramatically depleted, but rejuvenate easily, and that no studies have been done on the impact of coral. He says these surveys are done the world over and we have seen no real decimation of the oceans. There are many scientists that disagree. We investigate the science and the motivation behind Shell’s move on our shores. Summary: After a 9 year hiatus, exploration for gas reserves through 3D seismic surveys is planned to start on the 1st of December this year, by Royal Dutch Shell PLC, on South Africa’s Wild Coast. The scope of the survey will cover more than 6000 square kms at depths of 700m to 3000m. The exploration area is about 20 kilometers from the coastline at it’s closest point. Shell plans to embark on this seismic survey off the coast between Morgan Bay in the south and Port St Johns in the North. Over 150 000 South Africans have put pen to paper and signed a petition against this invasion of our shores. More protests are planned and marine biologists and activists are ready to serve an urgent interdict to try and stop this. But Shell says it’s within it’s legal right to conduct this survey based on an EMPr conducted in 2013. This is especially pertinent in light of the fact that at the COP26 conference an $8,5 Billion deal was signed to help South Africa move away from reliance on fossil fuels, and Royal Dutch Shell has been ordered to reduce its emission by 45% by 2030 compared to 2019 levels. The case was brought against Shell by Friends of the Earth Netherlands, a climate advocacy group that has waged similar lawsuits in the past to accelerate global climate action. Shell plans to appeal the decision. The ruling requires the company to transform its business model worldwide, cutting emissions both for its own operations and the products it sells. Basically the company is being forced to reduce its production and sale of fossil fuels, so why is Shell continuing its exploration on South African shores? Surveys of this nature can take up to 20 years to become drilling sites should gas be discovered and this is at a time that the world is moving away from fossil fuel energy. So who stands to benefit and who stands to lose? We investigate the long term effects of this decision. Further information: Nearly 200 concerned environmental defenders arrived at the Cape Town Waterfront on November 21 to protest against Shell’s seismic testing vessel Amazon Warrior, as it made its way into Cape Town harbour. The Amazon Warrior was commissioned by Shell to conduct seismic testing off the Wild Coast, in the Eastern Cape, stretching from the Kei river to the uMtamvuna river on the border of KwaZulu-Natal. The vessel will conduct seismic surveys for an estimated five months. This is an incredibly sensitive narrow coastal shelf along the East Coast of South Africa which is home to some of the most undisturbed natural areas and Marine reserves in the country including Dwesa, Cwebe and Hluleka reserves. Not only this but the Wild Coast is notorious for some of the most extreme weather conditions and is recognised as one of the most treacherous coasts in the world due to its narrow continental shelf, strong ocean currents and severe wind conditions which have caused many ships to be lost over the years. Any future installation of oil rigs would place the entire coastline at risk of environmental destruction if anything were to happen in these treacherous waters. Shell Exploration and Production SA which is a part of Royal Dutch Shell Plc issued a statement earlier this year, on their “Drive for net-zero emissions…” which outlines their stated objective of reducing their carbon footprint whilst supporting low environmental impact products, this surely doesn’t form part of that objective. Shell has issued a statement: Shell Downstream South Africa (Pty) Corporate Reputation and Media Relations spokesperson Pam Ntaka, said a full stakeholder consultation process was undertaken as part of the development of the EMPr for this project in 2013. “Furthermore, the Environmental Authorisation was obtained for this project in 2014,” Ntaka said. “… An Environmental Compliance audit was undertaken in 2020 by independent specialists to confirm that the controls and mitigation measures outlined in the EMPr were still sufficient and valid.” “… The audit report confirmed that these requirements were still sufficient and valid for this project to be taken forward. We can confirm we are operating within our legal right and we believe we have met all our obligations concerning the survey,” Ntaka said. “… Shell had a long experience in collecting seismic data and the welfare of wildlife was a major factor in the stringent controls it uses, strictly following the international guidelines of the Joint Nature Conservation Committee. We take great care to prevent or minimize impacts on fish, marine mammals and other wildlife. This is an exercise to collect data to help us understand if there is oil/gas or not. This is not a drilling exercise.” The Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment (DFFE) on November 22 said Mineral Resources and Energy Minister Gwede Mantashe was responsible for the administration of the Mineral and Petroleum Resources Development Act (MPRDA) and that Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment Minister Barbara Creecy was, therefore, not mandated to consider an application or to make a decision on the authorisation of a seismic survey being undertaken by oil and gas multinational Shell. “The impact of the seismic survey to be undertaken by Shell and [impact investment organisation] Impact Africa has been authorised under the MRPDA, which, under Section 39 (2) of the MPRDA requires the submission of an environmental management plan, which is to assess and evaluate the environmental impacts of the activity.” “… Since the coming into effect of the One Environment System on December 8, 2014, the application process for the seismic surveys was finalised. All decisions made under the MPRDA at the time remain valid and binding until set aside by a court of law,” the DFFE said in a statement. ENVIRONMENTAL MANAGEMENT PLAN Meanwhile, these marine protection practices during seismic surveying align with the findings and recommendations of an unrelated ‘Environmental Management Plan for a reconnaissance permit to undertake a speculative two-dimensional (2D) seismic survey in the Durban Basin off the East Coast of South Africa’, prepared by local environmental consultancy CCA Environmental for State-owned petroleum exploration Petroleum Agency South Africa (Pasa) in October 2013. This 2013 environmental management plan (EMP) said that, in summary, the majority of the impacts associated with the seismic survey would be of short-term duration and limited to the immediate survey area. As a result, the majority of the impacts associated with the seismic survey are considered to be of very low to low significance after mitigation. “The two key issues identified in this study relate to the potential impact on turtles and marine mammals, including physiological injury and behavioural avoidance, as a result of seismic noise; and the potential impact on the fishing industry, including vessel interaction, disruption to fishing operations and reduced catch, owing to the presence of the survey vessel, potential fish avoidance of the survey area and changes in feeding behaviour,” the report's authors said. “Although most of the impacts on turtles and cetaceans [whales, dolphins and porpoises] are assessed to have very low to low significance with mitigation, the impact could be of much higher significance owing to the limited understanding of how short-term effects of seismic surveys relate to longer term impacts,” the report highlighted. “For example, if a sound source displaces a species from an important feeding or breeding area for a prolonged period, impacts at the population level could be more significant. In order to mitigate the potential impact on turtles and cetaceans it is recommended that the proposed seismic survey be planned to avoid key turtle nesting periods, from October to March, with peak nesting during December and January, and cetacean migration and breeding periods from the beginning of June to end of November. “Thus, from an ecological perspective, the proposed survey should be undertaken from mid-March to the end of May. However, should the applicant require a longer survey period, that is early March to mid-June, the survey programme should be scheduled to avoid inshore areas during early March and the southern area during June”, the CCA Environmental 2013 EMP said. TREATMENT AND APPROACH I have spoken to both Kevin Cole, Natural Scientist and Simon Elwen, Marine Biologist who have differing opinions of how serious the impact is of seismic surveys. Although Simon Elwen is still advising the legal team who are bringing about the interdict against Shell, so clearly he is not that comfortable with it. I have been approached by many organisations who are willing to assist in filming protests etc and have been offered a seat on the Bateleurs on the 5th of December where there will be protests along the coast. I can make a plan to have those filmed even if I don’t take that seat. Interviews with both scientists as well as concerned citizens. There is also an international scientist I am trying to get hold of who has done a study on how seismic blasiting devastates the ocean’s zooplankton, which are critical food sources for marine mammals: Francine Kershaw, Staff Scientist. Marine Mammals, Oceans Division, Nature Program, USA. Environmental protection and small-scale fishing lobby organisation The Green Connection strategic lead Liz McDaid said Shell has used a legal loophole, as no environmental impact assessment was required in 2013 and this authorisation was being used to justify its actions in 2021. Liz was involved in halting the nuclear deal, and she is concerned about the impact on fishing. She is willing to speak to us. Judy Mann International Advisor for aquariums around the world, and a member of the South African Association for Marine Biological Research. Sinegugu Zukulu – Activist Wild Coast – Amadiba Crisis Committee, an initiator of the protests for the 5th of December. He is an internationally recognised environmentalist and cultural expert. Nonhle Mbuthuma – Activist against mining. (Has been involved in the struggle against mining in Xolobeni for years). Ricky Stone – Attorney for bringing about the interdict on behalf of various organisations. I have been in contact with him and he is passing on information, although right now they are busy with the urgent interdict, but he is willing to be interviewed. Another element I am exploring is following the money, what I know so far but still need to verify is that ANC owns 51% of Thebe and Thebe has 28% of Shell Downstream. I have to look deeper into that. HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 24 February 2022 Press Release: Globally the time for oil and gas exploration is running out and South Africa's oceans have been carved up - with seismic surveys mapping out our oceans - the Wild Coast is marked. Can its unique marine life remain unscathed? Script: Shots of underwater sea life (whale song) whales, dolphin sea creatures swimming… Simon: Yeah, absolutely. The oceans are incredibly noisy. // BEAT!!! ANIMALS Simon: A lot of the animals that live on the water, communicate acoustically // BEAT// ANIMALS Simon: And that's because sound travels better than anything else underwater, //BEAT//ANIMALS Music visuals INTERRUPT WITH LOUD ENGINE NOISE OF THE BOAT..CONTINUE NOISE OF BOAT.. UNDER LINK AND FADE OUT UNDER LINK: Most of us are super sensitive to noise, be it to the neighbour playing loud music, the guy in the four-by-four hooting behind us. What do we know about noise underneath the water affecting marine life? VO: The voices of marine experts can give us an inkling Simon: What's a core focus with marine mammals is that they use sound also for navigation, because the dolphins and the beaked whales, they echolocate. VO: Marine biologist Dr Simon Elwen, director of Seasearch, studies the behaviour and acoustic communication of these sound-sensitive beings. Simon: They use sound to find food as well as to communicate with other individuals. SEISMIC BANG!!! VO:-Now what happens if this connection gets disrupted? AIRGUNS BLASTING IN THE WATER VO: Disrupted by 3D Seismic survey airguns fired from a ship into the water - Exploring the ocean bed for oil and gas. //BEAT//BLASTS Moving along a straight line gathering data, each seismic array pulse emits a sound that lasts less than 0.1 seconds at source and is repeated every 10 to 20 seconds. // BEAT// WITH BLAST Simon: And these, make an incredibly loud noise in the region of 200 decibels underwater, VO: On land 200 decibels is louder than a jet engine taking off, but in water, the amplification, reception, and experience of sound are varied across species, because each is sensitive to different frequencies. Derek: We going to look at some seals. I mean, how would they be affected by those air guns? Simon: So if animals do have their hearing injured, that is obviously quite a negative impact. They use it in their day-to-day communication for mothers to find pups and vice versa Derek: Simon, I'm trying to equate this to living in a block of apartments with a neighbor's drilling on his wall every 10 seconds. I’d go crazy! Simon: And it really gets complicated when you're looking at whole ecosystems, you know, the loud noise like drilling next door, it might not kill you, but it might make you use that room less or, or Derek:.. move somewhere else, Simon: or even just eat a little bit less every day. And that that can become really important for species that are on the edge or endangered. //BEAT// SOUND UP PROTESTS. LINK: When South Africans heard about the 3d seismic surveys along the pristine wild coast, there was an outcry against the possible impact on marine life and that reverberated across the country. VO: Petroleum giant Shell SA was embarking on a five-month exploration for oil and gas starting in December 2021, spanning 6000 square kilometres. Neville: The next thing I saw, there was 1000s of people on that beach, you know, and the people were singing and dancing and chanting. SOUND UP DEMONSTRATIONS VO: Community coordinator for the Green Connection, Neville van Rooy was on the ground. Neville: And it was communities from the area that came out. because our livelihood is connected to the ocean, our culture is connected to the ocean, our heritage is connected to the ocean. VO: Shell's failure to consult with some small-scale fishing communities and directly affected people in the area tipped the scales. On the 28th of December last year a court stopped the seismic survey in its tracks. But this was not the end of the legal process, Shell is appealing. Attorney Wilmien Wicomb is representing the communities. Derek: So we’re celebrating a battle, but the war isn't over? Wilmien: That's certainly the case. Although I do think it was quite a punch in the nose for Shell. VO: How this clash unfolds hinges on an Environmental Authorisation //BEAT//- which Shell does not have. This only became law in December 2014 under the National Environmental Management Act, NEMA. Phindile: So that Shell authorization, was applied for and granted under the MPRDA, as was the legislation at that time VO: Regulating the industry is the Petroleum Agency South Africa, PASA. CEO Phindile Masangane maintains the 2013 permit is valid Phindile: So we could not have granted them authorization under an existing legislation, and then turn around and say, Actually, you've got to redo it, because now we've got new regulations. The Department of the Environment also agrees with us in this instance. VO: But one doesn't have to look far to see there is more to the relationship between Shell and the governing party. Even though this permit is for Shell's upstream business which involves exploration and production, it could be argued when it comes to shareholding there may be a conflict of interest. The Batho Bhatho Trust, an investment vehicle for the ANC, is about a 46 percent shareholder of Thebe Investment Corp, and Thebe owns 28% of Shell's downstream business, the processing aspect of oil and gas, in South Africa. In December, the Batho Batho Trust donated R15 million to bail out the ANC to pay its salaries. We put it to Hloniphizwe Mtolo, Country Chair of Shell South Africa. Derek: There is a financial connection between Shell and the ANC/government and they regulate your permit. Surely your international compliance officers must be concerned about a conflict of interest. Hloniphizwe: We dispute very strongly the connection between Shell, the ANC, and government. What we do in terms of permitting, we follow the rules to the letter Derek: It's a fine line, isn't it? Hloniphizwe: Not in this particular case, In this particular case. We are looking at a shareholder who is working with a different part of the business and we are working on upstream. Derek: But basically if Shell thrives, so does the ANC/Government, simple as that. Hloniphizwe: We don't know that, and we don't believe that. But we believe that if this activity is successful South Africa will benefit Wilmien: On the face of it, there's a serious conflict. But it has not arisen in any of the cases but, you know, watch this space. Phindile: To try and find a link between any commercial relationship between the ANC and Thebe investment, as well as this production, right, I think I think it is stretching it. LINK: Shell believes that they have complied with the conditions of the exploration permit and have taken enough precautions to mitigate any irreparable environmental damage. Hloniphizwe: South Africa, in the last five years, there has been at least 12 seismic surveys that have been done. And all of those were done safely. Hloniphizwe: The survey that we've started, we've done at least 14%, of what we wanted to do. And there has been absolutely no harm to the environment. VO: The exclusion zone is meant to lessen damage to sea life. Shell has extended it beyond the compulsory 500 meters to 800 meters Hloniphizwe That means that if an animal gets into this exclusion zone, the actual activity gets stopped. On a 24 hour basis, this zone is monitored. This survey that we were conducting in the wild coast is, has the lowest sound levels of any seismic survey that's been conducted in the past. VO: But these mitigations are not enough for Dr Jean Harris who leads the marine programme Wild Oceans for Wild Trust. Jean: We know from scientific studies where trained observers were looking for humpback whales that up to 40% were being missed. So what's happening to the rest of them? VO: Wild Oceans was concerned when Shell decided to start the Seismic survey in December - at the tail end of the Humpback whale migration. Jean: Reported evidence is that animals can lose connection with each other between, for example, a humpback whale and her calf. So it would have been much more responsible to start the survey in January, and then to move through to May at maximum. VO: Elwen insists more research is needed for South African waters. He is also frustrated by public misconceptions on the impact of seismic surveys Simon: They have not been linked clearly to killing whales and dolphins, they clearly have behavioural impacts they mask the communication of animals, there are many negative impacts, but it doesn't result in mass strandings of animals VO: We dropped anchor in a quiet stretch of sea to listen on hydrophones to what's going on beneath. Simon: You can still hear the ship in the background. And you can also hear crackling noise and that crackling's snapping shrimp SOUND UP: DEREK LISTENING TO CRACKLING SHRIMP - SEA SEARCH SOUND LIBRARY / Snapping Shrimp from remote location (Vema Seamount) - Sea Search Sound Library.mp3 Derek: I can hear the crackling. VO: A reminder of the less audible and less visible creatures in the path of seismic surveys. Amongst them - zooplankton, an integral part of marine ecosystems. // In an Australian 2017 study published in Nature Ecology & Evolution, the devastating effects on zooplankton could be seen up to a 1.2-kilometre range. Jean: the zooplankton, the small crustacea, and other species, which are the bottom of the food web. If you look at what they look like, after the shockwave has come through, there was, dead dead ones, damaged ones, indicating that, you'd have a mortality or death on those species. VO: Wrong place, wrong time. Many marine animals could find themselves in the seismic danger zone, like critically endangered turtle species whose nestlings are swept along the Cape Agulhas current in the months of January to March. Derek: There's also seen to be harmful effects on dolphins, turtles, and other sea creatures. Hloniphizwe 31:28 From our evidence, there hasn't been any damage to those other creatures, we take great care in making sure that if there is any impact, it is impact that is as small as possible. Derek: Mr. Mtolo, nobody's doing turtle tracking surveys, post your seismic operations. So we don't really know, Hloniphizwe: What we do do, after the survey is completed, is to go back there and investigate if there's any any damage that has taken place. We do that with each and every one of the surveys that we do. Derek: Do you really? Hloniphizwe: We do Derek: With a separate ship? Hloniphizwe: Yeah, it would be a post-survey ship. Derek: Can you give us examples of some of the ships that go in afterwards? Hloniphizwe: We can, I can get you that information. VO: But the devil's in the detail - on request for clarification after the interview it appears Mtolo was mistaken, there is no post-survey ship. Shell says all monitoring and reporting is in real-time from the vessels conducting the actual survey because they're always on the move. So without any reliable data after the survey ship has left the area, the knock-on effects are hard to quantify. LINK: You have to ask the question, why is the exploration for oil and gas which can take up to a decade or more, and encourages the use of fossil fuels being supported by government? Phindile: It is Eskom the operator of the grid, that is saying it is very, very important for them to bring sufficient gas generated electricity to stabilise the grid. VO: And government wants South Africa to have its own supply, under the Gas Master Plan, transitioning from an electricity supply system dominated by coal, to renewable energy supplemented by gas. So even though South Africa committed to reducing its Carbon Footprint in global climate agreements, it has carved up its oceans for large-scale oil and gas exploration. Wilmien: No one is taking a step back and trying to understand the cumulative impact of all these different permits. They're looking at them one by one. And that I think is really going to be a disaster. VO: Well we've reached our destination - Seal Island - A Priceless haven SPLASH - DEREK INTO THE WATER SLO-MO VO: For South Africa the economic benefits at this point are uncertain. The landscape for Minister Gwede Mantashe's "Gas Master Plan" is becoming more of a battleground, possibly at the expense of these trusting creatures.

The Green Connection is particularly concerned about the timing of this seismic survey phase, which is understood to still fall within the migration season for hump-backed whales and warned it could also endanger juvenile turtles coming down the coast in the Agulhas current and into the survey area over the five-month period. Shell’s own 2013 Environmental Management Programme (EMPr) states that it should try to “avoid surveying during December when humpback whales may still be moving through the area on their return migrations”, McDaid pointed out. Scientists are at loggerheads, some like Kevin Cole say, that not enough research has been conducted to really understand the impact of seismic surveys, and Simon Elwen who was involved in the original EMPr says that it’s not as devastating as people are making out, although there are behavioural impacts on marine life but according to him, they are short term. He does admit that Zooplankton are dramatically depleted, but rejuvenate easily, and that no studies have been done on the impact of coral. He says these surveys are done the world over and we have seen no real decimation of the oceans. There are many scientists that disagree. We investigate the science and the motivation behind Shell’s move on our shores.
metadata.Summary: After a 9 year hiatus, exploration for gas reserves through 3D seismic surveys is planned to start on the 1st of December this year, by Royal Dutch Shell PLC, on South Africa’s Wild Coast. The scope of the survey will cover more than 6000 square kms at depths of 700m to 3000m. The exploration area is about 20 kilometers from the coastline at it’s closest point. Shell plans to embark on this seismic survey off the coast between Morgan Bay in the south and Port St Johns in the North. Over 150 000 South Africans have put pen to paper and signed a petition against this invasion of our shores. More protests are planned and marine biologists and activists are ready to serve an urgent interdict to try and stop this. But Shell says it’s within it’s legal right to conduct this survey based on an EMPr conducted in 2013. This is especially pertinent in light of the fact that at the COP26 conference an $8,5 Billion deal was signed to help South Africa move away from reliance on fossil fuels, and Royal Dutch Shell has been ordered to reduce its emission by 45% by 2030 compared to 2019 levels. The case was brought against Shell by Friends of the Earth Netherlands, a climate advocacy group that has waged similar lawsuits in the past to accelerate global climate action. Shell plans to appeal the decision. The ruling requires the company to transform its business model worldwide, cutting emissions both for its own operations and the products it sells. Basically the company is being forced to reduce its production and sale of fossil fuels, so why is Shell continuing its exploration on South African shores? Surveys of this nature can take up to 20 years to become drilling sites should gas be discovered and this is at a time that the world is moving away from fossil fuel energy. So who stands to benefit and who stands to lose? We investigate the long term effects of this decision.
metadata.Further information: Nearly 200 concerned environmental defenders arrived at the Cape Town Waterfront on November 21 to protest against Shell’s seismic testing vessel Amazon Warrior, as it made its way into Cape Town harbour. The Amazon Warrior was commissioned by Shell to conduct seismic testing off the Wild Coast, in the Eastern Cape, stretching from the Kei river to the uMtamvuna river on the border of KwaZulu-Natal. The vessel will conduct seismic surveys for an estimated five months. This is an incredibly sensitive narrow coastal shelf along the East Coast of South Africa which is home to some of the most undisturbed natural areas and Marine reserves in the country including Dwesa, Cwebe and Hluleka reserves. Not only this but the Wild Coast is notorious for some of the most extreme weather conditions and is recognised as one of the most treacherous coasts in the world due to its narrow continental shelf, strong ocean currents and severe wind conditions which have caused many ships to be lost over the years. Any future installation of oil rigs would place the entire coastline at risk of environmental destruction if anything were to happen in these treacherous waters. Shell Exploration and Production SA which is a part of Royal Dutch Shell Plc issued a statement earlier this year, on their “Drive for net-zero emissions…” which outlines their stated objective of reducing their carbon footprint whilst supporting low environmental impact products, this surely doesn’t form part of that objective. Shell has issued a statement: Shell Downstream South Africa (Pty) Corporate Reputation and Media Relations spokesperson Pam Ntaka, said a full stakeholder consultation process was undertaken as part of the development of the EMPr for this project in 2013. “Furthermore, the Environmental Authorisation was obtained for this project in 2014,” Ntaka said. “… An Environmental Compliance audit was undertaken in 2020 by independent specialists to confirm that the controls and mitigation measures outlined in the EMPr were still sufficient and valid.” “… The audit report confirmed that these requirements were still sufficient and valid for this project to be taken forward. We can confirm we are operating within our legal right and we believe we have met all our obligations concerning the survey,” Ntaka said. “… Shell had a long experience in collecting seismic data and the welfare of wildlife was a major factor in the stringent controls it uses, strictly following the international guidelines of the Joint Nature Conservation Committee. We take great care to prevent or minimize impacts on fish, marine mammals and other wildlife. This is an exercise to collect data to help us understand if there is oil/gas or not. This is not a drilling exercise.” The Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment (DFFE) on November 22 said Mineral Resources and Energy Minister Gwede Mantashe was responsible for the administration of the Mineral and Petroleum Resources Development Act (MPRDA) and that Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment Minister Barbara Creecy was, therefore, not mandated to consider an application or to make a decision on the authorisation of a seismic survey being undertaken by oil and gas multinational Shell. “The impact of the seismic survey to be undertaken by Shell and [impact investment organisation] Impact Africa has been authorised under the MRPDA, which, under Section 39 (2) of the MPRDA requires the submission of an environmental management plan, which is to assess and evaluate the environmental impacts of the activity.” “… Since the coming into effect of the One Environment System on December 8, 2014, the application process for the seismic surveys was finalised. All decisions made under the MPRDA at the time remain valid and binding until set aside by a court of law,” the DFFE said in a statement. ENVIRONMENTAL MANAGEMENT PLAN Meanwhile, these marine protection practices during seismic surveying align with the findings and recommendations of an unrelated ‘Environmental Management Plan for a reconnaissance permit to undertake a speculative two-dimensional (2D) seismic survey in the Durban Basin off the East Coast of South Africa’, prepared by local environmental consultancy CCA Environmental for State-owned petroleum exploration Petroleum Agency South Africa (Pasa) in October 2013. This 2013 environmental management plan (EMP) said that, in summary, the majority of the impacts associated with the seismic survey would be of short-term duration and limited to the immediate survey area. As a result, the majority of the impacts associated with the seismic survey are considered to be of very low to low significance after mitigation. “The two key issues identified in this study relate to the potential impact on turtles and marine mammals, including physiological injury and behavioural avoidance, as a result of seismic noise; and the potential impact on the fishing industry, including vessel interaction, disruption to fishing operations and reduced catch, owing to the presence of the survey vessel, potential fish avoidance of the survey area and changes in feeding behaviour,” the report's authors said. “Although most of the impacts on turtles and cetaceans [whales, dolphins and porpoises] are assessed to have very low to low significance with mitigation, the impact could be of much higher significance owing to the limited understanding of how short-term effects of seismic surveys relate to longer term impacts,” the report highlighted. “For example, if a sound source displaces a species from an important feeding or breeding area for a prolonged period, impacts at the population level could be more significant. In order to mitigate the potential impact on turtles and cetaceans it is recommended that the proposed seismic survey be planned to avoid key turtle nesting periods, from October to March, with peak nesting during December and January, and cetacean migration and breeding periods from the beginning of June to end of November. “Thus, from an ecological perspective, the proposed survey should be undertaken from mid-March to the end of May. However, should the applicant require a longer survey period, that is early March to mid-June, the survey programme should be scheduled to avoid inshore areas during early March and the southern area during June”, the CCA Environmental 2013 EMP said. TREATMENT AND APPROACH I have spoken to both Kevin Cole, Natural Scientist and Simon Elwen, Marine Biologist who have differing opinions of how serious the impact is of seismic surveys. Although Simon Elwen is still advising the legal team who are bringing about the interdict against Shell, so clearly he is not that comfortable with it. I have been approached by many organisations who are willing to assist in filming protests etc and have been offered a seat on the Bateleurs on the 5th of December where there will be protests along the coast. I can make a plan to have those filmed even if I don’t take that seat. Interviews with both scientists as well as concerned citizens. There is also an international scientist I am trying to get hold of who has done a study on how seismic blasiting devastates the ocean’s zooplankton, which are critical food sources for marine mammals: Francine Kershaw, Staff Scientist. Marine Mammals, Oceans Division, Nature Program, USA. Environmental protection and small-scale fishing lobby organisation The Green Connection strategic lead Liz McDaid said Shell has used a legal loophole, as no environmental impact assessment was required in 2013 and this authorisation was being used to justify its actions in 2021. Liz was involved in halting the nuclear deal, and she is concerned about the impact on fishing. She is willing to speak to us. Judy Mann International Advisor for aquariums around the world, and a member of the South African Association for Marine Biological Research. Sinegugu Zukulu – Activist Wild Coast – Amadiba Crisis Committee, an initiator of the protests for the 5th of December. He is an internationally recognised environmentalist and cultural expert. Nonhle Mbuthuma – Activist against mining. (Has been involved in the struggle against mining in Xolobeni for years). Ricky Stone – Attorney for bringing about the interdict on behalf of various organisations. I have been in contact with him and he is passing on information, although right now they are busy with the urgent interdict, but he is willing to be interviewed. Another element I am exploring is following the money, what I know so far but still need to verify is that ANC owns 51% of Thebe and Thebe has 28% of Shell Downstream. I have to look deeper into that.
